title: Mistakes at work

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Luqman, the servant who ate the bitter melon and remembered the sweet. Your line was calm under orders.

The report has already gone out to the whole team, and the totals at the bottom are wrong. Nobody has noticed yet. There's a small window, about the length of a coffee, when the mistake belongs only to its maker. It could be fixed quietly. It could be left to see if anyone spots it. Or there's a hard message to send, just three words long: that was me. Old texts from two very different places speak to that window. Today: Zigong.
screen: `THE TOTALS ARE WRONG.` → `A SMALL WINDOW.` → `THAT WAS ME.`

segments.voice: First, Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy." Two moves after the mistake: confess it, say it out loud; forsake it, stop doing it. What doesn't prosper isn't the mistake. It's the covering. Second, Confucius. In the Analects he says, more or less: to have a fault and not change it, that is what's really called a fault. The first slip is ordinary; hands slip. The real fault, for Confucius, comes after, in the refusal to change. Third, his student Zigong adds a picture. A noble person's faults, he says, are like eclipses of the sun and moon. When he errs, everyone sees it. When he changes, everyone looks up to him. An eclipse doesn't hide. It happens in full view, it passes, and the light comes back where everyone can see it. Fourth, putting it to work. Own it, fix it, learn: the phrase is modern, but the old texts hold each step. Confess is owning it. Forsake is fixing it and not repeating it. Change is learning. At work, it fits in two plain sentences. I got that wrong. Here's what I'm doing about it. No speech, no long account of why it wasn't really your fault. Just the eclipse, in full view, and then the light.
screen: `CONFESS AND FORSAKE.` · `THE REAL FAULT IS NOT CHANGING.` · `FAULTS LIKE ECLIPSES.` · `OWN IT, FIX IT, LEARN.` · then, large: `I GOT THAT WRONG.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one recent mistake, at work or at home, nothing dramatic, and notice the urge to explain it, soften it, make it smaller, then let that pass by. Silently try the plain sentence, I got that wrong, and name one small fix and one thing you'd do differently next time. If someone should hear it, let their face come to mind; if you pray, you can bring the mistake to God in your own tradition's words.
Zigong. Confucius's student who said a noble person's faults are like eclipses: seen by all, then lit again when changed. Today's word.
Your line: own it. A fault in full view passes, like an eclipse. Day nine hundred twenty, done.

howItsDone: Readers of the Analects return to its sayings on faults as a guide to self-correction, and Jews and Christians read Proverbs 28:13 as a call to confess wrongs and turn from them.

chat.says: I made a mistake nobody's noticed yet. Should I just fix it quietly?
options: Say it plainly first: I got that wrong, here's the fix. Covering it is the real problem.
Yes. If you fix it before anyone notices, it was never really a fault at all.
Fix it quietly. Owning up only makes sense if somebody else spots it first.
chat.meaning: Proverbs says whoever covers his sins won't prosper; Confucius says the real fault is not changing. Own it, fix it, learn.
